title: The village
hookLine: he walked to town often; Walden was a short walk from Concord, and his mother fed him sometimes

lines: THE PATH OUT OF THE WOODS.
cards: "Every day or two I strolled to the village to hear some of the gossip." That's Thoreau, in Walden, the book known as the story of a man alone in the woods. Every day or two, a walk into town.
Not a secret he got caught keeping: he gave it a chapter of its own, right in the middle of the book, and called it The Village. The cabin was real. So was the path out of the woods.

teach.b: First, the setup. Walden opens with Thoreau living alone in the woods, "a mile from any neighbor," in a house he built himself. That's the picture that sticks.
A mile is real distance on foot. It's also a walk you can make before lunch. Second, what he went for.
He went to hear the gossip, he says, and taken in small doses it was as refreshing in its way as the rustle of leaves and the peeping of frogs. He's not apologizing.
People are part of the landscape too, and he watched the villagers the way he watched the pond. Third, the walk home.

teach.h: HOME BY FEEL IN THE DARK.
teach.b: He describes leaving town late, sometimes on dark nights, and finding his way back through the woods by feel, his feet knowing the path when his eyes couldn't. The village and the woods weren't two worlds.

They were two ends of one walk. Fourth, the help. Some readers like to point out, sometimes as a joke at his expense, that his family's house in Concord was close by, and tradition says he ate there now and then.
It's easy to make that a gotcha. But there's another way to hear it.
Nobody really lives alone. Thoreau's experiment in living simply still had a mother, a town, a cobbler and a road under it. Being honest about that doesn't shrink the experiment.
It makes it something an ordinary person could try.

how: Readers of Walden often notice that Thoreau's solitude sat close to a town he visited often, and take it as a reminder that even a simple, independent life rests on other people.

games.why: every day or two, he says, he walked to the village. he watched the people the way he watched the pond.

practice: Quietly, start counting what holds you up, not in a grand way: the person who taught you to cook, the friend who answers late, the bus driver, the water from the tap, the shop that has bread.
Let each one come and go with a breath, and if you pray, hold them there for a moment. There's no need to feel anything in particular; just notice how long the list gets.
